questions.text: Which phase of a compiler converts the source text into a stream of tokens?
questions.solution: The lexical analyser groups characters into the smallest meaningful units, identifiers, keywords, literals and operators, and hands them to the parser.

questions.text: In which phase is a type mismatch such as adding an integer to a string detected?
questions.solution: The expression is lexically and grammatically fine, so only the phase that reasons about meaning, using the symbol table, can catch it.

questions.text: What is the correct order of the compiler phases?

options.text: Lexical, syntax, semantic, intermediate code, optimisation, code generation
Syntax, lexical, semantic, code generation, optimisation
Lexical, semantic, syntax, optimisation, code generation
Lexical, syntax, intermediate code, semantic, code generation

questions.solution: Each phase consumes the output of the one before: characters to tokens, tokens to a parse tree, the tree checked for meaning, then intermediate code, improved, and finally target code.

questions.text: What does a lexical analyser produce as output?
questions.solution: It returns tokens, usually as a token name plus an attribute value, and enters identifiers into the symbol table as it goes.

questions.text: Which of the following is normally discarded by the lexical analyser rather than returned as a token?
questions.solution: Comments and whitespace only separate tokens and carry no meaning for the parser, so they are skipped. Removing them here is why the grammar need not mention them at all.

questions.text: How many tokens does a C lexical analyser produce for the following line?  printf("i=%d, &i=%x", i, &i);
questions.solution: The tokens are printf, (, the whole string literal, comma, i, comma, &, i, ), and the semicolon: 10 in all. The commas and the ampersand inside the quotes are part of the single string token, not separate tokens.

questions.text: The patterns recognised by a lexical analyser are most naturally specified using
questions.solution: Tokens form regular languages, so regular expressions suffice and can be compiled into a finite automaton that scans in linear time. Nesting, which needs a stack, is left to the parser.

questions.text: The output of the syntax analysis phase is

options.text: a parse tree or syntax tree

questions.solution: The parser checks that the token stream matches the grammar and records the derivation as a tree, which the later phases walk.

questions.text: The syntax of programming language constructs such as nested expressions is described using
questions.solution: Balanced nesting cannot be described by a regular language, so a context-free grammar is needed. The pushdown stack of a parser is exactly the extra power required.

questions.text: A bottom-up parser constructs the parse tree

options.text: from the leaves upward to the root
from the root downward to the leaves
left to right without a tree

questions.solution: It starts from the input symbols and reduces them to non-terminals until the start symbol is reached, which traces a rightmost derivation in reverse.

questions.text: Which family of parsers is also described as shift-reduce parsers?
questions.solution: LR parsers work by shifting tokens onto a stack and reducing a handle on top of it by a production. The LL family is predictive and top-down.

questions.text: Handle pruning is the basis of
questions.solution: A handle is a substring matching the right side of a production whose reduction is a step in a rightmost derivation reversed. Repeatedly finding and reducing handles is what bottom-up parsing does.

questions.text: A context-free grammar is ambiguous if

options.text: some string in its language has more than one parse tree
it has more than one non-terminal

questions.solution: Ambiguity is about the grammar admitting two distinct derivation trees for one string, which leaves the meaning of that string undetermined.

questions.text: The dangling-else problem is an instance of
questions.solution: With nested if statements and one else, the grammar allows the else to attach to either if. Languages resolve it by a rule, usually matching the else to the nearest unmatched if.

questions.text: Deciding whether an arbitrary context-free grammar is ambiguous is
questions.solution: No algorithm can decide ambiguity for every grammar. In practice a parser generator reports the conflicts it finds, which is a sufficient but not necessary sign of trouble.

questions.text: Recursive descent parsing is a form of
questions.solution: Each non-terminal becomes a procedure that tries to match its production, so the tree is built from the start symbol downward.

questions.text: A grammar containing left recursion cannot be parsed by
questions.solution: A production such as A -> A a makes a recursive descent parser call itself without consuming input, so it loops forever. Left recursion must be eliminated first; bottom-up parsers handle it happily.

questions.text: A grammar fails to be LL(1) when

options.text: two productions for the same non-terminal have overlapping FIRST sets, or a nullable production whose FIRST meets the FOLLOW set
it has more than one terminal
it has epsilon productions of any kind

questions.solution: An LL(1) parser picks a production from one lookahead token, so the choices must be distinguishable. Overlapping FIRST sets, or a FIRST and FOLLOW clash for a nullable non-terminal, put two entries in one table cell.

questions.text: An SLR(1) parser decides to reduce by a production A -> alpha when the lookahead is in

options.text: the lookahead recorded in the item itself

questions.solution: SLR uses the global FOLLOW set as its reduction lookahead. Because FOLLOW is computed without regard to context, it is coarser than the per-item lookaheads that CLR carries.

questions.text: Which ordering of parser power is correct?

options.text: SLR(1) is weaker than LALR(1), which is weaker than CLR(1)
CLR(1) is weaker than LALR(1), which is weaker than SLR(1)
All three accept exactly the same grammars
LALR(1) is the most powerful of the three

questions.solution: Every SLR(1) grammar is LALR(1) and every LALR(1) grammar is CLR(1). The trade-off is table size: CLR has the most states, and LALR gets close to its power with an SLR-sized table.

questions.text: A shift-reduce conflict in a parsing table means that

options.text: in some state with some lookahead, the parser can neither be told to shift nor to reduce unambiguously
the input contains a lexical error

questions.solution: One table entry holds two possible actions, so the parser cannot decide. It signals that the grammar is not in the class the table was built for, often because of ambiguity.

questions.text: An LALR(1) parsing table is obtained from a CLR(1) table by

options.text: merging states that have the same core of LR(0) items
replacing FOLLOW sets by FIRST sets
removing left recursion from the grammar

questions.solution: States differing only in their lookaheads are combined and their lookahead sets unioned, which shrinks the table to the size of an SLR table.

questions.text: Merging CLR(1) states to form an LALR(1) table can introduce

options.text: reduce-reduce conflicts, but never shift-reduce conflicts
shift-reduce conflicts, but never reduce-reduce conflicts

questions.solution: Merging only unions lookaheads for reductions, which can make two reductions compete. Shift actions depend on the core items, which merging leaves unchanged, so no new shift-reduce conflict can appear.

questions.text: Parser generators such as YACC and Bison produce which kind of parser by default?
questions.solution: LALR(1) is the practical compromise: nearly the power of CLR(1) with a much smaller table, which mattered greatly when these tools were written.

questions.text: A three-address code instruction contains at most

options.text: one operator with two operands and one result

questions.solution: The three addresses are two operands and a destination, so complex expressions are broken into a sequence with temporaries. That regular shape is what makes later analysis and code generation simple.

questions.text: How many three-address statements are needed for a = b * c + d * e, if each intermediate product uses a new temporary and the final sum is assigned directly to a?
questions.solution: t1 = b * c; t2 = d * e; a = t1 + t2. Each statement carries one operator, which is what forces the temporaries.

questions.text: Which of these is a standard implementation of three-address code?
questions.solution: A quadruple stores operator, two operands and result; a triple drops the result field and refers to instructions by position. Indirect triples add a level of indirection so code can be reordered easily.

questions.text: A basic block is

options.text: a maximal sequence of instructions entered only at the first and left only at the last

questions.solution: Control cannot jump into the middle or out of the middle, so every instruction in the block runs whenever the first one does. That property is what makes local optimisation within a block safe.

questions.text: The first instruction of a basic block is called
questions.solution: Leaders are the first instruction of the program, any target of a jump, and any instruction immediately following a jump. Each block runs from a leader up to just before the next one.

questions.text: In a control flow graph, what do the nodes represent?
questions.solution: Nodes are basic blocks and edges show the possible transfers of control between them. Working at block granularity keeps the graph small enough for data flow analysis.

questions.text: Common subexpression elimination is an example of
questions.solution: It works on the intermediate representation and needs no knowledge of the target machine. Register allocation and instruction scheduling are the machine-dependent counterparts.

questions.text: Dead code elimination removes

options.text: computations whose results are never used
unreferenced variables from the symbol table
the last statement of every block

questions.solution: If a value is never read on any path afterwards, computing it cannot affect the result. Liveness analysis is what establishes that.

questions.text: Replacing the expression 3 * 4 by 12 at compile time is called
questions.solution: Folding evaluates an operation whose operands are already known. Propagation is the related step of carrying a known constant to the places where the variable is used, which often exposes more folding.

questions.text: Loop-invariant code motion

options.text: moves a computation whose operands do not change out of the loop
converts a for loop into a while loop

questions.solution: If nothing the expression depends on is modified inside the loop, it computes the same value every iteration and can be hoisted into a pre-header so it runs once.

questions.text: Replacing a multiplication inside a loop by a repeated addition on an induction variable is called
questions.solution: An expensive operator is swapped for a cheaper one that produces the same sequence of values. Array address arithmetic is the classic case: i * width becomes a running sum.

questions.text: Peephole optimisation examines

options.text: a short window of neighbouring instructions at a time
one basic block at a time

questions.solution: A small sliding window is matched against a set of replacement patterns. The narrow view is what makes it cheap, and repeated passes let one improvement expose another.

questions.text: Which is a typical peephole transformation?

options.text: Deleting a load that immediately follows a store to the same location
Rewriting the grammar to remove left recursion
Allocating registers across the whole function

questions.solution: The value is already in the register, so the reload is redundant. Other stock patterns are removing jumps to the next instruction and algebraic simplifications such as adding zero.

questions.text: Peephole optimisation is usually applied
questions.solution: It cleans up the local inefficiencies that code generation introduces, and it can also be run on intermediate code. Either way it comes after the code is emitted, not before.

questions.text: A symbol table stores

options.text: identifiers together with attributes such as type, scope and storage location
the tokens of the program in order

questions.solution: It is the compiler's record of what each name means, built during lexical and syntax analysis and consulted heavily during semantic analysis and code generation.

questions.text: Which data structure gives the best average-case lookup time for a symbol table?
questions.solution: Hashing gives constant average lookup, which matters because the table is consulted for nearly every identifier occurrence. Nested scopes are handled by chaining a table per scope.

questions.text: In syntax-directed translation, semantic rules are attached to
questions.solution: Each production carries rules computing attribute values, so the translation is defined alongside the grammar and evaluated as the parse tree is built.

questions.text: An attribute whose value is computed only from the attributes of a node's children is called
questions.solution: Synthesised attributes flow upward and can be evaluated during a bottom-up parse, which is why S-attributed definitions suit LR parsing. Inherited attributes take values from the parent or siblings.
